% Appendix: Quantization Robustness (SF2 response)
% exp_ids: sf2_qwen_int4_scierc_s1, sf2_llama_int4_scierc_s1,
%          sf2_qwen_int4_docred_s1, sf2_llama_int4_docred_s1,

\section{Quantization Robustness}
\label{app:quantization}

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.2pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrr rrr@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Qwen3-8B}} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Llama-3.1-8B}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-4} \cmidrule(l){5-7}
& FP16 & INT4 & $\Delta$ & FP16 & INT4 & $\Delta$ \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{7}{@{}l}{\textit{SciERC (551 docs)}} \\[2pt]
DR\,(\%)\,$\downarrow$  & 0     & 0     & 0      & 0.09  & 0     & $-$0.09 \\
R-F1\,$\uparrow$ & 43.77 & 41.71 & $-$2.06 & 45.47 & 43.98 & $-$1.49 \\
E-F1\,$\uparrow$ & 67.05 & 67.05 & 0.00   & 67.76 & 67.54 & $-$0.22 \\
\addlinespace[4pt]
\multicolumn{7}{@{}l}{\textit{DocRED (200 docs)}} \\[2pt]
DR\,(\%)\,$\downarrow$  & 0     & 0     & 0      & 0     & 0     & 0 \\
R-F1\,$\uparrow$ & 40.79\textsuperscript{\dag} & 40.07 & $-$0.72 & 47.35 & 48.04 & $+$0.69 \\
E-F1\,$\uparrow$ & 81.87\textsuperscript{\dag} & 74.84 & $-$7.03\textsuperscript{\ddag} & 85.43 & 84.18 & $-$1.25 \\
PF\,(\%) & 8.5\textsuperscript{\dag}  & 18.5  & $+$10.0\textsuperscript{\ddag} & 2.0   & 2.5   & $+$0.5 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\caption{FP16 vs.\ INT4 (AWQ) quantization under LoRA + S1 on SciERC and DocRED. F1 $\times$ 100; PF = parse-failure rate.
\textsuperscript{\dag}Qwen DocRED FP16 evaluated on 998 docs (all other configurations use matched subsets).
\textsuperscript{\ddag}E-F1 drop primarily attributable to increased parse failures under INT4 quantization on long documents rather than constraint interference (DR remains 0\%).}
\label{tab:quantization}
\end{table}

INT4 (AWQ) quantization preserves constraint enforcement across both datasets: DR remains at 0\% for all four model--dataset configurations under INT4, with the sole FP16 violation (Llama SciERC, 0.09\%) disappearing after quantization.
R-F1 changes range from $-$2.06 to $+$0.69\,pp, consistent with expected quantization quality costs independent of the constraint layers.
On DocRED, Qwen INT4 exhibits elevated parse failures (18.5\% vs.\ 8.5\% FP16) due to timeout on long documents under quantized inference; the resulting E-F1 gap ($-$7.03\,pp) reflects generation-length degradation rather than constraint-layer interference, as DR remains 0\%.
These results provide indirect evidence that the 70B AWQ INT4 results (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}) are not confounded by quantization artifacts in the constraint enforcement mechanism.

Table~\ref{tab:prompt-sensitivity} shows that constrained decoding eliminates entity-type and relation-vocabulary violations entirely (ET and RV drop to 0\%) for all prompt variants at both scales. At 8B, domain-range violations are reduced by 94.0\%--94.6\% with a standard deviation of only 0.3\,pp across prompts; F1 scores remain effectively unchanged (max shift 0.13\,pp R-F1).

At 70B, constrained decoding achieves DR${=}$0\% across all three prompts ($\Delta$DR${=}$100\%), consistent with the scale-dependent semantic layer interaction observed in the main experiments (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). Baseline DR varies widely (0.22\%--6.41\%), yet constrained decoding converges to zero in all cases; CF is introduced as expected (0.62\%--3.50\%), consistent with the per-triple enforcement trade-off.

Prompt variation has a measurable effect on baseline (unconstrained) violation rates at both scales: 8B DR ranges from 11.1\% (Detailed) to 16.9\% (Minimal); 70B from 0.22\% to 6.41\%. Under constrained decoding, this variance collapses, confirming that the mechanism is orthogonal to prompting and generalizes without prompt-specific tuning.

% exp_id: sf2_70b_prompt_sensitivity
\paragraph{LoRA fine-tuned prompt invariance.}
Under LoRA fine-tuning at 70B, prompt invariance is preserved: Minimal and Detailed prompts both achieve DR${=}$0\% under S1, with CF at 0.62\% and 0.75\% respectively---consistent with the zero-shot 70B pattern above.
This confirms that OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is robust to prompt variation across both zero-shot and fine-tuned regimes.

## 1. Claim 强度评估

### 当前 claim 强度合理，有 2 个被低估的数据点

**已充分利用的核心 claim：**
- DR≤0.21% + R-F1 ±0.3pp：数据充分，表述准确 ✓
- 非加性组合 3%+24%→94%：论文最独特发现，§7 已正确强调 ✓
- beam k=4 消除所有违规 at 8B：准确，有 "at 8B" 限定 ✓
- 70B 84% vs 8B 24%："preliminary single-family" 限定恰当 ✓

**被低估的 2 个数据点（不需要新实验，只需要写作强调）：**

1. **"被约束移除的 triples 中 97.6-100% 是 false positives"**（§5 L88 括号里一笔带过）
   - 这是论文最强的"免费午餐"论据：约束几乎不损失任何正确预测
   - 当前位置：§5 composability 段括号内 "removed triples are 97.6--100\% false positives"
   - 建议：提升到 §1 intro 中，与 "R-F1 ±0.3pp" 并列。"Constraints are effectively free: 97.6-100% of removed triples are false positives, with only 1/514 (0.2%) false negatives blocked"
   - 对审稿人"你的约束会不会伤害召回"的预期攻击是最强回应

2. **"514 个 FN 中仅 1 个 (0.2%) 被约束阻止"**（§5 L146）
   - 与上一点互补：从 FP 和 FN 两侧证明约束无害
   - 当前位置：§5 downstream impact 段
   - 可作为 §1 的一句话增强

**不建议修改：** DDL 46h 内改 abstract/intro 引入新的表述风险大于收益。如果 freeze 前有最后一次编辑机会，优先级是这两个点。但如果已经 freeze，不改也可以。

### Claim 过强/过保守检查

- **过保守**：Abstract "reduces DR to ≤0.21%"——实际 Qwen SciERC 达到 DR=0%，但 ≤0.21% 是跨所有 config 的保守上界，保留是正确的
- **恰当**：所有 70B claim 都有 "preliminary/single-family" 限定 ✓
- **恰当**：F1 范围 "40-46%" 与 PL-Marker 41.6% 对比，不声称 SOTA ✓
- **无过强 claim**

## 2. Story 优化空间

### 叙事线评估：连贯，无断裂

Problem（15-18% violations）→ Gap（GCD 无跨字段感知 / post-hoc 丢弃 15-74%）→ Method（decidability → two-layer）→ Key finding（非加性 3+24→94）→ Scale（70B 84%）→ Deployment tiers（greedy/beam-2/beam-4）

每一步都有数据支撑，逻辑链完整。§7 已正确以实证发现（非加性组合）开头，不是 Proposition 1。

### R26 扣分点修复评估

| 扣分点 | 修复前 | 修复后 | 评估 |
|--------|--------|--------|------|
| Claim 精度 | ">90% total reduction" 无支撑 | "26-52% greedy S1; beam k=4 eliminates all" | ✓ 已修 |
| Abstract 过度 | Raw percentage | Severity-framing | ✓ 已修 |
| 70B single-family | 未标注 | "preliminary single-family" + "speculative hypothesis" | ✓ 已修 |
| Position→name gap | Case 1 不适用 name-based | 补充 PDA 无法随机访问论证 | ✓ 已修 |
| GoLLIE/PL-Marker 数字 | 无来源或来源错误 | ACE05 63.6-70.1% + PL-Marker 41.6% 正确引用 | ✓ 已修 |
| Mistral scope | C1 未区分 ZS/FT | "additionally under LoRA fine-tuning" 限定 | ✓ 已修 |

### 残余攻击面（3 个，按严重性排序）

**A. [中] Table 2 无 error bars / std**
Table 2 是 greedy deterministic 解码（T=0），所以 std=0 是合理的。但审稿人可能不理解这一点。当前 caption 说 "No ΔR-F1 is significant (Bonferroni-corrected)"——bootstrap CI 在正文提及但不在表中。
→ 防御：Table 2 caption 可以加一句 "Greedy decoding (T=0) yields deterministic outputs; reported CIs are bootstrap over documents"

**B. [中] 单家族 70B + 无 GoLLIE 组合实验**
声称 "orthogonal and complementary to GoLLIE" 但没有 GoLLIE+OntoCoDec 实验。审稿人可能要求验证。
→ 防御：Appendix GoLLIE comparison 已经论证了方法论差异，且 GoLLIE 在 SciERC 上 R_F1=0，组合实验无意义。

**C. [低] Greedy S1 总违规减少 26-52%**
这是论文中最弱的数字。审稿人可能问 "constraints 只减少了一半违规？"
→ 已防御：severity-framing（DR irrecoverable → CF correctable）比 raw percentage 更有说服力。beam k=4 作为 ultimate solution 也已提及。

## 3. GPU 实验 ROI 评估

### 总体建议：不跑新实验

DDL 46h 内跑新实验的风险显著高于收益。论文已 submission-ready。新实验可能：
- 产生弱结果（如 Mistral FT 因 calibration 差导致 DR 残余高），反而削弱论文
- 引入新数据不一致（未经充分验证的数字进入论文）
- 挤占 final compile / 匿名仓库推送的时间

### 候选逐个评估

| 候选 | 预期评分提升 | 执行风险 | 时间成本 | 推荐 |
|------|-------------|---------|---------|------|
| Qwen-72B 跨家族 | 高（C3→cross-family） | 高（下载35GB+适配+调试） | 28-32h | ❌ 风险太高 |
| Mistral LoRA | 中（Table 2 +1行） | 中（Mistral ZS 56.9% DR，FT 可能不佳） | 6-8h | ❌ 弱结果风险 |
| ACE05 新数据集 | 中（+1 dataset） | 极高（全新 pipeline） | 12-20h | ❌ 不可能 |
| M2 CF bootstrap CI | 低（error bars） | 极低（纯分析） | 2-3h | ⚠️ 可选但收益小 |
| 70B PS 写入 | 已完成 | 无 | 0h | ✅ 已在 appendix |

### 如果一定要做一件事

M2 CF bootstrap CI 是唯一安全的候选：
- 不涉及 GPU，纯 Python 分析
- 为 Table 2 的 CF 列添加 95% CI
- 执行风险接近零
- 但评分提升有限（R26 未明确要求 CF error bars）

**我的建议：不做。将精力集中在确保 final compile 零错误 + 匿名仓库推送。**

## 总结

论文在当前状态下是 solid Findings-level（3.0-3.5），R26 修复有效提升了写作精度。距离 Conference（4.0）的核心差距是：
1. 单家族 70B（需要 cross-family，DDL 内不可行）
2. 缺少与 GoLLIE/KnowCoder 的 head-to-head 组合实验（registry 显示 GoLLIE R_F1=0，组合无意义）

这两个差距在 DDL 前无法安全弥补。建议 freeze + 提交。如果被分到 Findings，这两点可以在 camera-ready 或 rebuttal 中补充。

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B on both RE datasets under fine-tuning (1.39$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations decreasing $\sim$31\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item Systematic ablation across 3 model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) and 2 datasets (SciERC, DocRED) in zero-shot settings; Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B additionally under LoRA fine-tuning, demonstrating DR reduction to $\leq$0.21\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.3\,pp; DR enforcement introduces CF as a correctable side effect (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}).
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework grounded in the observation that domain/range type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars---grammar-only approaches face state spaces of $6^{17}$--$6^{19}$ for typical IE schemas (Proposition~1; \S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types.
    \item Preliminary single-family scale exploration on Llama-3.1-70B (AWQ INT4), revealing a scale-dependent layer interaction: the semantic layer alone achieves 84\% DR reduction at 70B vs.\ 24\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). At 8B, beam $k{=}2$ is Pareto-optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.18$\times$ greedy S1 latency); $k{=}4$ achieves DR${=}$0\% with near-zero CF at 1.39$\times$.
\end{enumerate}

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B on both RE datasets under fine-tuning (1.39$\times$ latency).
Constraint enforcement is effectively lossless: 97.6--100\% of removed triples are false positives, and only 1 of 514 false negatives (0.2\%) is attributable to constraints (\S\ref{sec:downstream-impact}).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations decreasing $\sim$31\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item Systematic ablation across 3 model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) and 2 datasets (SciERC, DocRED) in zero-shot settings; Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B additionally under LoRA fine-tuning, demonstrating DR reduction to $\leq$0.21\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.3\,pp; DR enforcement introduces CF as a correctable side effect (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}).
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework grounded in the observation that domain/range type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars---grammar-only approaches face state spaces of $6^{17}$--$6^{19}$ for typical IE schemas (Proposition~1; \S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types.
    \item Preliminary single-family scale exploration on Llama-3.1-70B (AWQ INT4), revealing a scale-dependent layer interaction: the semantic layer alone achieves 84\% DR reduction at 70B vs.\ 24\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). At 8B, beam $k{=}2$ is Pareto-optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.18$\times$ greedy S1 latency); $k{=}4$ achieves DR${=}$0\% with near-zero CF at 1.39$\times$.
\end{enumerate}
